cards: Genghis Khan, born Temüjin in 1162, was the founder of the Mongol Empire.
Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant and traveller who lived in China between 1275 and 1292 during the Yuan Dynasty.
Philip II of France, known as Philip Augustus, was king of France from 1180 to 1223.
Louis IX of France, king from 1226 to 1270, was revered as a model Christian ruler and canonised in 1297.
Charles I of Anjou was the youngest brother of Louis IX of France, Count of Anjou and of Provence through his marriage to Beatrice of Provence in 1246.
Ottokar II was king of Bohemia from 1253, known as the Iron and Golden King for his military strength and wealth.
Rudolf I of Germany, a Swabian count of the Habsburg family, was elected King of the Romans in 1273, ending the Great Interregnum after the fall of the Hohenstaufen.
Batu Khan was a grandson of Genghis Khan and founder of the Golden Horde.
Roger of Lauria was an admiral in the service of the Crown of Aragon and Sicily, regarded as one of the greatest naval commanders of the Middle Ages.
Alexander Nevsky was a Rus' prince who served as prince of Novgorod and from 1252 as Grand Prince of Vladimir.
Albert of Riga was a canon of Bremen who became bishop of Livonia in 1199 and led the crusade against the pagan peoples of the eastern Baltic.
Snorri Sturluson was an Icelandic chieftain, lawspeaker and author of the Prose Edda and the Heimskringla, a history of the kings of Norway.
Iltutmish was a Turkic slave commander who seized the throne of Delhi in 1211.

Thomas Aquinas was a thirteenth-century Italian Dominican friar and theologian, the most influential philosopher of medieval scholasticism.
Henry of Livonia was a priest who took part in the German crusades in the eastern Baltic and wrote the Livonian Chronicle, covering events to 1227.
Henry III was king of England from 1216, succeeding his father John as a nine-year-old.
Muhammad of Ghor was a ruler of the Ghurid dynasty who conquered much of northern India in the late twelfth century.
Kertanegara was the last king of Singhasari in eastern Java.
Rumi, Jalal al-Din Muhammad, was a Persian poet, Sufi mystic and scholar born in Balkh in 1207.
As-Salih Ayyub was an Ayyubid prince who ruled Hisn Kayfa and the Jazira before becoming sultan of Egypt in 1240.
Conradin was the last legitimate member of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, Duke of Swabia and claimant to the kingdoms of Sicily and Jerusalem.
Al-Kamil was an Ayyubid sultan of Egypt who reigned from 1218 to 1238, a nephew of Saladin.
Konrad I of Masovia was a Polish duke of the Piast dynasty, ruling Masovia and Kuyavia and briefly holding Kraków.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, known as Llywelyn the Last, was prince of Gwynedd and the only native ruler formally recognised by England as Prince of Wales, by Henry III in the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267.
Peter II was king of Aragon and count of Barcelona from 1196.
Ram Khamhaeng was the third king of Sukhothai, reigning from about 1279 to 1298, under whom the Thai kingdom expanded widely.
Béla IV of Hungary was king from 1235 to 1270.
James I, called the Conqueror, was king of Aragon and count of Barcelona from 1213 to 1276.
Mangrai was the founder of the northern Thai kingdom of Lan Na.
Mindaugas was the first known Grand Duke of Lithuania and its only crowned king.
Ramon Llull was a philosopher, mystic and missionary from Majorca, born soon after the Aragonese conquest of the island.
David VI Narin was king of Georgia, crowned as co-ruler with his cousin David VII Ulu under Mongol overlordship.
Kaidu was a Mongol prince, a grandson of Ögedei, who dominated Central Asia from 1272 to 1301.
Kayqubad I was sultan of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia from 1220 to 1237, the period of its greatest power.
Muhammad I of Granada, known as Ibn al-Ahmar, was the founder of the Nasrid dynasty and the Emirate of Granada.
Pope Boniface VIII, born Benedetto Caetani, was pope from 1294 to 1303.
William of Modena was an Italian churchman and papal legate in the Baltic lands from the 1220s.
Al-Adil was the brother of Saladin and sultan of the Ayyubid realm from 1200 to 1218.
Bernat Desclot was a Catalan chronicler of the late thirteenth century.
Ibn Hud, Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Hud al-Mutawakkil, claimed descent from the Hudids of Zaragoza and rose against the Almohads in 1228 in the Ricote valley near Murcia.
